p108: 108.  The Group of Academic Experts submitted that no multilateral treaty expressly prohibited the use of amnesties for international crimes. It explained that the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) interpreted Article 6 § 5 of Additional Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions in a manner suggesting that States could not grant amnesty to persons suspected of, accused of or convicted of war crimes. However, an analysis of the travaux préparatoires of that Article showed that the only States which had raised the question of the perpetrators of international crimes, namely the former USSR and some of its satellite States, had linked that issue to that of foreign mercenaries. The third-party intervener found it curious that the ICRC interpreted Article 6 § 5 as excluding from its scope only war criminals and not the perpetrators of other international crimes, given that the statements of the former USSR on which the ICRC relied had, in its view, specifically provided for the prosecution of those guilty of crimes against humanity or crimes against peace. The Group of Academic Experts failed to see what arguments would justify excluding war criminals, but not the perpetrators of genocide or crimes against humanity, from the potential scope of amnesties. Furthermore, the ICRC referred to examples of non-international conflicts such as those which had taken place in South Africa, Afghanistan, Sudan and Tajikistan, even though the amnesties associated with those conflicts had all covered at least one international crime.
p109: 109.  The third-party intervener referred to the difficulties encountered in negotiating amnesty clauses in treaties (citing the 1998 Rome Conference which led to the establishment of the International Criminal Court (ICC), the negotiations on the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance, and the 2012 Declaration of the High-level Meeting of the General Assembly on the Rule of Law at the National and International Levels). Those difficulties were indicative of the lack of consensus among States on the issue.
p110: 110.  The third-party intervener relied on a body of scholarly writing on amnesties which, in its view, tended to show that since the Second World War States had increasingly resorted to amnesty laws. While acknowledging that the number of new amnesty laws excluding international crimes was on the increase, it maintained that the same was true of the number of amnesties granted for such crimes. Amnesties were the most frequently used form of transitional justice. The use of amnesties in peace agreements concluded between 1980 and 2006 had remained relatively stable.
p111: 111.  In the third-party intervener’s view, even though several international and regional courts had expressed the view that international law prohibited amnesties in cases of international crimes, the authority of such judicial decisions was weakened by their lack of consistency as to the scope of that prohibition and the crimes to which it applied. The Group of Academic Experts cited the example of the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, which had stated in Barrios Altos, cited above, that all amnesty provisions were inadmissible because they were intended to prevent the investigation and punishment of those responsible for human rights violations, whereas in Massacres of El Mozote and nearby places, cited above, the President of that court and four other judges had qualified that position by acknowledging that, even in cases of gross human rights violations, the obligation to prosecute was not absolute and had to be weighed against the requirements of peace and reconciliation processes in post-conflict situations.
p112: 112.  Moreover, a number of national supreme courts had upheld their countries’ amnesty laws, considering that such laws contributed to the establishment of peace, democracy and reconciliation. The third-party intervener cited the following examples: the findings of the Spanish Supreme Court in the trial of Judge Garzón in February 2012; the decision of the Ugandan Constitutional Court declaring the Amnesty Act 2000 constitutional; the refusal of the Brazilian Supreme Court in April 2010 to annul the 1979 Amnesty Law; and the upholding by the South African Constitutional Court, in the AZAPO case, of the constitutionality of the Promotion of National Unity and Reconciliation Act 1995, which provided for broad recourse to amnesty.
